title: Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF)

assessment.name: Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF)
assessment.description: The Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF) is a 28-item self-report measure of sexual motivation for adults aged 18 years and over (Meston et al., 2020). It assesses the reasons a person has engaged in sex, capturing how frequently each of 14 distinct motivations has led them to have sexual intercourse across their past sexual experiences. For respondents who have not previously had sex, the measure instead assesses the likelihood that each motivation would lead them to have sex.

administration.instructions: People have sex (i.e., sexual intercourse) for many different reasons. Below is a list of some of these reasons. Please indicate how frequently each of the following reasons led you to have sex in the past. If you have not had sex in the past, use the scale to indicate the likelihood that each of the following reasons would lead you to have sex. I have had sex in the past because… Response scale (same for every item): 1 = None of my sexual experiences; 2 = A few of my sexual experiences; 3 = Some of my sexual experiences; 4 = Many of my sexual experiences; 5 = All of my sexual experiences.
administration.form_scope: One selected archived form. Other editions and related forms remain separate source assets.

source_rule_excerpts: Internal consistency was assessed in a validation sample of 223 United States adults recruited online (ages 19 to 76, median 33; Meston et al., 2020, Study 2). The two-item subscale alphas ranged from .42 to .93, with an average of .74. Reliability was strongest for Reproduction (α = .93), Mate Guarding (α = .82), Resources (α = .81), Stress Reduction (α = .80), and Physical Desirability (α = .80), and acceptable for most remaining subscales, including Love and Commitment (α = .78), Social Status (α = .76), Experience Seeking (α = .75), Duty/Pressure (α = .75), Self-Esteem Boost (α = .74), and Revenge (α = .70). Pleasure (α = .68) and Expression (α = .62) showed more modest internal consistency, and Practical was the weakest subscale (α = .42), reflecting its two items spanning distinct physical and emotional benefits.

source_guidance.title: YSEX-SF Scoring
source_guidance.text:
All 28 items have response options ranging from 1 (None of my sexual experiences) to 5 (All of my sexual experiences). Each of the 14 subscales is scored by summing its two items, giving subscale scores from 2 to 10. Higher scores indicate that a greater proportion of the respondent’s sexual experiences have been motivated by that reason.
No total score is computed, and the measure has no norms, percentiles, or clinical cut-offs. The clinical output is the 14-subscale profile. For respondents who have not had sex, the instructions direct them to rate the likelihood that each reason would lead them to have sex, and their profile is read as anticipated rather than experienced motivation.
Subscale | Items | What it assesses
Stress Reduction | 1, 15 | Sex used to release frustration, anxiety, or stress. Higher scores may indicate that sex serves an emotion-regulation function.
Pleasure | 2, 16 | Sex motivated by physical enjoyment and desire. Typically among the most frequently endorsed motivations.
Physical Desirability | 3, 17 | Sex motivated by attraction to the other person’s appearance. The items refer to the person rather than a partner, reflecting that the measure covers casual and non-partnered sex.
Experience Seeking | 4, 18 | Sex pursued for novelty, adventure, or excitement.
Resources | 5, 19 | Sex exchanged for tangible gain such as money or favours. Elevated scores indicate that exchange-based motivations feature in the respondent’s experiences.
Reproduction | 6, 20 | Sex motivated by the desire to conceive. Scores are strongly context-dependent and interpreted in light of life stage and relationship circumstances.
Social Status | 7, 21 | Sex used to enhance reputation or standing.
Revenge | 8, 22 | Sex used to retaliate against a partner or get even with someone. Elevated scores may indicate unresolved relational conflict.
Practical | 9, 23 | Sex pursued for practical benefits. The two items span distinct content, one physical and one emotional, so reviewing them individually shows which is driving the score.
Love and Commitment | 10, 24 | Sex used to express love and feel connected. Low scores in a partnered respondent may be clinically informative about the relational function of sex.
Expression | 11, 25 | Sex used to mark special occasions or transitions, such as welcomes, farewells, and celebrations.
Self-Esteem Boost | 12, 26 | Sex used to feel better about oneself. Elevated scores may indicate that sexual activity is serving a self-worth regulation function.
Duty/Pressure | 13, 27 | Sex engaged in out of obligation or in response to pressure. Elevated scores can reflect experiences of sexual coercion.
Mate Guarding | 14, 28 | Sex used to keep a partner from straying. Elevated scores may indicate relationship insecurity or fear of abandonment.

source_guidance.title: Interpreting the YSEX-SF Profile
source_guidance.text:
The profile is interpreted relatively. The most clinically informative feature is which motivations are most and least frequent for the respondent, rather than the value of any single subscale in isolation. Considered together, the 14 subscale scores describe the overall shape of the respondent’s motivational profile.
Conceptually related subscales are often more informative in combination than any subscale considered alone. Representative examples include:
Frequent Duty/Pressure alongside frequent Mate Guarding may indicate that sex is functioning to preserve a relationship in which the person feels insecure, directing attention toward relational safety and communication.
Frequent Stress Reduction alongside frequent Self-Esteem Boost may indicate that sex is serving an emotion-regulation or self-worth function.
Frequent Pleasure, Love and Commitment, and Expression together describe sexual activity that is intrinsically and relationally motivated.
Infrequent Pleasure or Love and Commitment in a partnered respondent presenting with sexual dissatisfaction may itself be the clinically salient finding.

source_guidance.title: YSEX-SF Norms
source_guidance.text: NovoPsych does not calculate YSEX-SF percentiles. The only available normative data come from the validation sample of 223 United States adults recruited online, reported separately by gender, with pronounced floor effects on several subscales because most respondents endorse None of my sexual experiences for motivations such as Resources, Revenge, and Reproduction. Percentiles derived from that sample would imply a reference comparison and a degree of precision the data do not support. The measure also has no clinical cut-offs anywhere in the literature. Interpretation therefore rests on the frequency descriptors and the shape of the profile.

source_guidance.title: Should clinicians focus on the highest-scoring subscale?
source_guidance.text: Not necessarily. The pattern across subscales is often more informative than any single score. Most people report a combination of motivations rather than a single dominant reason, and results are best interpreted alongside the client’s history, presenting concerns, and broader clinical assessment.

reportScoringGuidance.text:
Each of the 14 subscales is scored by summing its two items (response options 1 'None of my
sexual experiences' to 5 'All of my sexual experiences'), giving subscale scores from 2 to 10.
Higher scores indicate that a greater proportion of the respondent's sexual experiences have
been motivated by that reason. No total score is computed and no norms, percentiles, or clinical
cut-offs exist; the clinical output is the 14-subscale profile.
Each subscale score is accompanied by a frequency descriptor derived from the response
options (score 2 = 'None of my sexual experiences'; 3-4 = 'A few'; 5-6 = 'Some'; 7-8 = 'Many';
9-10 = 'All of my sexual experiences'). These descriptors are frequency labels, not severity
ratings: the clinical relevance of a given frequency depends on the motivation being assessed
and the respondent's circumstances.
The profile is interpreted relatively: the most clinically informative feature is which motivations
are most and least frequent for the respondent, rather than the value of any single subscale in
isolation. If either Duty/Pressure item ('I was pressured into doing it', 'I felt obligated to') is
endorsed above 'None of my sexual experiences', the report displays a note for the clinician, as
motivations of this kind range from a sense of relational duty through to unwanted or coerced
experiences.
For respondents who have not had sex, the instructions direct them to rate the likelihood that
each reason would lead them to have sex, and their profile is read as anticipated rather than
experienced motivation.

sourceRequirements: No total score is computed, and the measure has no norms, percentiles, or clinical cut-offs.
NovoPsych does not calculate YSEX-SF percentiles.
Percentiles derived from that sample would imply a reference comparison and a degree of precision the data do not support.
The measure also has no clinical cut-offs anywhere in the literature.
Interpretation therefore rests on the frequency descriptors and the shape of the profile.

rows: Sex used to release frustration, anxiety, or stress. Higher scores may indicate that sex serves an emotion-regulation function.
Sex motivated by physical enjoyment and desire. Typically among the most frequently endorsed motivations.
Sex motivated by attraction to the other person’s appearance. The items refer to the person rather than a partner, reflecting that the measure covers casual and non-partnered sex.
Sex pursued for novelty, adventure, or excitement.
Sex exchanged for tangible gain such as money or favours. Elevated scores indicate that exchange-based motivations feature in the respondent’s experiences.
Sex motivated by the desire to conceive. Scores are strongly context-dependent and interpreted in light of life stage and relationship circumstances.
Sex used to enhance reputation or standing.
Sex used to retaliate against a partner or get even with someone. Elevated scores may indicate unresolved relational conflict.
Sex pursued for practical benefits. The two items span distinct content, one physical and one emotional, so reviewing them individually shows which is driving the score.
Sex used to express love and feel connected. Low scores in a partnered respondent may be clinically informative about the relational function of sex.
Sex used to mark special occasions or transitions, such as welcomes, farewells, and celebrations.
Sex used to feel better about oneself. Elevated scores may indicate that sexual activity is serving a self-worth regulation function.
Sex engaged in out of obligation or in response to pressure. Elevated scores can reflect experiences of sexual coercion.
Sex used to keep a partner from straying. Elevated scores may indicate relationship insecurity or fear of abandonment.
